study.locator: Designing an Effective Inference Engine: Continuous batching, with its orchestration of prefill and generate steps

study.title: Prefill and decode with the KV-cache
study.locator: Section 2.1, LLM Inference Process

focus: Prefill processes the whole prompt at once and writes one key-value pair per prompt token per layer; decode reads the full cache back for each new token and appends one pair.
TTFT covers scheduling delay plus prompt processing; per-token latency covers one decode step. Offline batch work cares about tokens per second, chat cares about both.
The manifest entries that move every estimate are layer count, hidden size, head counts with key-value heads, prompt and output lengths, batch size and precision.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the request path for the invented 64-layer model in the inference chapter's Worked Problems (D=4096, F=16384, N=32, K=8, H=256): total parameters 18.4e9, int8 key-value bytes per token 262,144, and the per-layer append of one [K, H] key plus one [K, H] value per new token. Derive both numbers from the manifest.
traps: Treating prefill and decode as one regime. Prefill is a batched parallel pass; decode is serial with cache reads, so one batch size or one roofline cannot cover both.
Counting tokens without naming prefill versus output tokens. Cost, latency and cache all scale with the two lengths differently.
Assuming batching speeds up every part. Batching reuses weights across requests, but each request adds its own key-value reads.

selfTest.q: A 512-token prompt arrives. What does prefill produce, and what does each decode step then read and write?
selfTest.a: Prefill processes all 512 tokens in parallel, writes 512 key-value pairs per layer and returns first-token logits. Each decode step reads the full cache, samples one token, and appends its pair.

selfTest.q: Which manifest entries must a shape manifest contain for this section's estimates?
selfTest.a: Layer count, hidden size, feed-forward size, query and key-value head counts with head dimension, prompt and output lengths, batch size, precision, and later the sharding.

selfTest.q: Why does batching raise linear-layer efficiency but not remove the decode bottleneck?
selfTest.a: Batching reuses each weight across requests, but every request adds its own key-value bytes, so cache traffic grows with batch while weight traffic does not.

selfTest.q: Which latency does a longer prompt directly worsen, TTFT or per-token latency?
selfTest.a: TTFT, through prompt processing time. Per-token latency is set by one decode step over weights plus cache.

study.depth: The attention scale is 1 over the square root of head dimension on the live page; if your copy renders it without the root, trust the root. The 2P rule is decode-only.

study.title: Key-value cache FLOP savings grow with sequence
study.locator: kv cache: the one-sixth saving paragraph and the no-cache quadratic paragraph

focus: One matmul through all parameters costs \(2P\) operations by the \(2mnp\) rule; the layer walk (qkv, output, MLP) sums to the same within 2%.
Decode attention per token scales with cached length (\(4SN_{\text{heads}}H\) per layer for scores plus values); prefill attention scales with prompt length squared.

Softmax, norms, sampling and the unembedding are \(O(d_{\text{model}})\) per layer against \(O(d_{\text{model}}^2)\) dense work; they matter only when the dense term shrinks or a profile says otherwise.
Use head count times head dimension, not model width, wherever key-value heads differ from query heads.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive decode operations per token for the invented 18.4e9-parameter model at cached length 8192: dense \(2 \times 18.4 \times 10^9 = 3.68 \times 10^{10}\), attention \(4 \times 8192 \times 32 \times 256 \times 64 = 1.72 \times 10^{10}\), total about \(5.4 \times 10^{10}\).
traps: Applying 2P to prefill. Prefill pays the dense term per prompt token plus quadratic attention; 2P per token describes one decode step.
Writing the attention scale as division by head dimension. The implemented scale is \(1/\sqrt{d_{\text{head}}}\); the count is unchanged but a kernel you write later must use the root.
Calling attention free in decode because 2P dominates. At 8192 cached tokens the invented model's attention is nearly half the dense count; recompute the share before dropping it.

selfTest.q: How many dense operations does one decode step take for the invented 18.4e9-parameter model?
selfTest.a: About \(3.68 \times 10^{10}\), from \(2 \times 18.4 \times 10^9\).

selfTest.q: At cached length 8192, what is its decode attention count, and what share is that?
selfTest.a: \(4 \times 8192 \times 32 \times 256 \times 64 = 1.72 \times 10^{10}\), nearly half the dense count, so it cannot be dropped there.

selfTest.q: Why is the 2P rule decode-only?
selfTest.a: It counts one token through stationary weights. Prefill runs all prompt tokens at once with quadratic attention, and sampling plus unembedding add their own terms.

selfTest.q: Without a cache, how does per-step work grow with sequence length n?
selfTest.a: Each step recomputes keys and values for all n tokens: \(2 \times 2 \times n \times L \times d^2\) operations, or n/6 of a full pass, so totals grow quadratically.

study.locator: What about memory? and Modeling throughput and latency for LLaMA 2-13B, including the parameter table and both batch tables
study.depth: The tables label memory GiB but divide decimal gigabytes by bytes per second (32.7e9 bytes at 6.56e12 bytes/s gives 4.98 ms). Recompute in bytes and keep GB apart from GiB.

study.title: Weights, key-value bytes per token and the capacity fit
study.locator: kv cache: the bytes-per-token formula; capacity
study.depth: Recompute both byte lines: 52e9 parameters at 2 bytes is 104e9 bytes (about 104 GB), and exact key-value bytes per token are 2,097,152. The article's rounded 0.002 GB per token gives about 28000 tokens on 4 GPUs, not the printed 23000; use your own number with a stated overhead.

study.title: Intermediate and workspace bytes
study.locator: intermediate memory costs: tensor contractions, statistical normalizations and element-wise operators, with GPU Kernel Fusion

focus: Parameters cost bytes-per-value times count under the stored precision; execution precision can differ (int8 weights with bf16 compute) and changes later intensities, not this line.

Key-value bytes per token are \(2 \times \text{bytes} \times L \times K \times H\); the \(4 \times L \times d_{\text{model}}\) shortcut assumes key-value width equals model width and breaks under GQA and MQA.
Activations are megabytes where the cache is gigabytes at 8k context (80 MB against 6.7 GB in the 13B example), but they still set the workspace and fragmentation overhead you must state.
Capacity fits subtract weights first, then divide by per-request cache; always add an overhead line for allocator, workspace and graphs instead of absorbing it into rounding.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the 13B bf16 cache at 8192 context (\(2 \times 2 \times 128 \times 40 \times 40 \times 8192 = 6.7 \times 10^9\) bytes), then the GQA variant with 8 key-value heads in int8 (81,920 bytes per token), then fit 8192-length requests beside 26 GB of weights on 8 16 GB cards (about 150).
traps: Reading the inference chapter's tables as GiB. The step times divide decimal gigabytes by bytes per second; recompute in bytes and keep GB apart from GiB.

Copying the article's 23000-token fit. Its own rounded 0.002 GB per token gives about 28000 (about 26700 with exact bytes); the printed 23000 carries an unstated discount, so publish your own overhead instead.
Calling activations negligible everywhere. They are negligible beside an 8k cache; at short context with large batch they set the workspace line.

selfTest.q: How many key-value bytes per token does the invented model (L=64, K=32, H=256) use in bf16?
selfTest.a: \(2 \times 2 \times 64 \times 32 \times 256 = 2{,}097{,}152\) bytes (2 MB); with K=8 in int8 it is 262,144 bytes.

selfTest.q: How many per token for a 40-layer, 8 key-value head, 128-dim model in int8?
selfTest.a: \(2 \times 40 \times 8 \times 128 = 81{,}920\) bytes (80 kB).

selfTest.q: Three 40 GB cards hold the 52B weights (104 GB). Can they serve batch 4 at 2048 tokens each?
selfTest.a: No. 16 GB remain, fitting about 7600 tokens against 8192 needed. Serve batch 3, shorten context, add a card, or shrink the cache.

selfTest.q: When does the per-token shortcut 4 x layers x model width fail?
selfTest.a: Whenever key-value width differs from model width: GQA and MQA need the explicit K and H entries.

study.title: The 208 ratio and per-stage flop-per-byte limits
study.locator: kv cache: Flops vs Memory Boundedness; batch sizes: the qkv/o/w1/w2 table
study.depth: The article writes the crossover as A_bw/A_f; read it as peak operations per second over bytes per second (312e12/1.5e12 = 208 FLOP/byte). Its 11% comms-latency remark does not reproduce from its own numbers (about 3 ms against 53 ms, near 6%); recompute instead of quoting.

focus: Intensity is operations over bytes moved (\(I = F/Q\)); the ridge is peak operations per second over bytes per second, and the bound is the minimum of the two ceilings.
A bf16 matmul with batch far below width has intensity near the batch size; the chapter's 240 on TPU v5e and 295 on H100 are the same ratio on different hardware.
Decode attention sits near \(I \approx 1\) FLOP/byte at one query token, so batch cannot move it; prefill attention sits near \(I \approx T/2\).
Report the lower (max) and upper (sum) bounds; the gap is the overlap assumption, and profiles decide it.
units.reproduce: Sweep bf16 [B, 4096] by [4096, 4096] on your GPU with event timing, warmup and interleaved repeats; plot achieved TFLOP/s against B and report the knee and the small-batch floor. Measured on an RTX 3050 Laptop GPU with PyTorch 2.14: plateau about 12 TFLOP/s, achieved copy bandwidth about 151 GB/s (ratio about 78 FLOP/byte), half the plateau near B=64, and one weight pass costing about 0.22 ms (33.6 MB at 151 GB/s). Your numbers will differ; the knee near your own measured ratio is the target.
traps: Quoting a ridge without naming the precision. int8 weights with bf16 compute halve the critical batch (120 versus 240 on v5e); int8 compute restores it.
Reading achieved peaks as vendor peaks. Dense H100 bf16 without sparsity is half the headline (9.89e14, not 1.979e15); measure your own plateau.
Expecting step time to fall with smaller batch below the knee. One full weight pass already costs about 0.22 ms here; batching toward the knee buys throughput, not latency.

selfTest.q: At what batch does a bf16 matmul turn compute-bound on H100, and why half the headline?
selfTest.a: About 295 (9.89e14/3.35e12). The headline 1.979e15 needs structured sparsity, so dense math uses half.

selfTest.q: What is decode attention intensity at one query token against a long cache, and what follows?
selfTest.a: About 1 FLOP/byte from ST/(S+T); it stays memory-bound at any batch, since each request adds its own cache bytes.

selfTest.q: On TPU v5e, past what prompt length is prefill attention compute-bound?
selfTest.a: Past about 480 tokens: intensity T/2 must clear the 240 ridge.

selfTest.q: State the lower and upper runtime bounds for the roofline int8 matmul question.
selfTest.a: Lower \(\max(T_{\text{math}}, T_{\text{comms}})\), upper their sum, with \(T_{\text{math}} = 2BDF/3.94 \times 10^{14}\) and comms bytes over 8.2e11 per second.

units.title: TTFT, TPOT, throughput and goodput
outcomes: Define TTFT, TBT, TPOT, normalized latency and capacity, and state what each hides (scheduling delay, jitter, prompt-length spread).
Compute fluidity-index for a timestamp trace and derive the fluid token generation rate at a stated SLO.
Show peak token throughput ranking two systems differently from SLO-qualified rate, using the paper's vLLM versus Sarathi-Serve and Groq numbers.
units.why: Throughput without a latency SLO ranks systems by their averages and hides the stalls users feel. SLO-qualified thinking is what turns a benchmark into a serving decision.

next.note: SLOs need the workload they hold under.
Record the SLO before the sweep, not after.

study.locator: Sections 2.2 and 3.1 with Figures 1 to 3 (the vLLM versus Sarathi-Serve arxiv_summarization comparison at 1.5 QPS)

study.title: fluidity-index, fluid rate and the two evaluation recipes
study.locator: Section 4.1 (Algorithm 1, Figure 4) and Section 4.2 (black-box and capacity recipes); Section 5.1 Figure 5 with Section 5.2 Figure 6
study.depth: The Start Here blurb promises a goodput methodology, but the paper defines no metric named goodput. Its SLO-qualified rates are fluid token generation rate and capacity under a fluidity SLO (99% of requests at 0.9 or higher). The text cross-reference to the algorithm is mistyped; read Algorithm 1 itself.

study.title: Latency-throughput tradeoff and cost per token
study.locator: What is the LLaMA Serving Story? through Visualizing the Latency Throughput Tradeoff, including the NumPy roofline snippet (kv_comms_time with attn_time always bandwidth-bound for generate)

focus: TTFT mixes scheduling delay with prompt processing and grows with prompt length (Figure 1, Yi-34B on 2 H100); never set it as one static SLO across lengths.
TPOT and normalized latency divide by decode count, so a 10 s stall over a 228-token median moves them by milliseconds; tail TBT sees the stall but not its timing or frequency.
fluidity-index banks early slack and resets deadlines after a miss (Algorithm 1, Figure 4); the fluid rate is the inverse of the smallest TBT deadline holding 99% of requests at 0.9 or higher.
The paper defines no metric named goodput despite the blurbs; cite fluid token generation rate and capacity for SLO-qualified throughput.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, score the Section 4 pair at TBT deadline 100 ms: both traces take one TBT miss in 11, while fluidity-index gives 1.0 to the 10 ms system and 10/11 to the 100 ms system. Derive both from Algorithm 1's slack and reset rules.
traps: Averaging TBT across requests. Means hide per-request stall timing; request-level deadline accounting exists because the CDFs and means disagreed (the P85 versus P99 flip in Figure 3c).
Fitting the prefill deadline on the wrong system. Dp comes from the evaluated system's isolated prefill curve (10 repeats), not from a constant or another engine's curve.
Reading Figure 5d as raw speed. It plots acceptance against TBT target at a fixed 10% miss line; Groq leads there while trailing on prefill in Figure 5c.

selfTest.q: What two components make up TTFT, and why can a short request show a large one?
selfTest.a: Scheduling delay plus prompt processing. Queueing behind earlier work inflates TTFT even when the prompt itself is cheap.

selfTest.q: Why must the prefill deadline Dp be a fitted function of prompt length?
selfTest.a: Prefill grows about quadratically (Figure 1), and the workload spreads 417 median to 1418 p90 tokens; a static target is either slack or impossible.

selfTest.q: The toy pair has TPOT 22.7 ms versus 104.5 ms, so TPOT separates them. Why is fluidity-index still needed?
selfTest.a: TPOT separates different means but hides stall structure at equal means: vLLM and Sarathi-Serve tie on TPOT while a 10 s stall wrecks one of them. Fluidity credits early slack and penalizes miss timing.

selfTest.q: How do the three Figure 5a rates rank Groq, and what does each assume?
selfTest.a: TPOT inverse gives about 600 tok/s (ignores stalls), tail-TBT inverse about 4x less (over-penalizes the tail), fluid rate sits between at the rate holding the 99%/0.9 SLO.

study.title: Medians, eviction and the prefill-generate ratio
study.locator: Median-length examples (prefill 8192 with decode 512 and 4096), the eviction math and the disaggregated prefill to generate ratio

focus: Report medians with spread, not points: 417 versus 1418 prefill tokens at median versus p90, 2k to 32k sliders, 24 hourly runs.
Cold pays tracing plus staged compilation, weight loading, allocator growth and autotuning; none of it belongs in a steady-state median.
Prefill length spread punishes whole-batch prefill (padding, blocking); eviction math (96 tokens per step at P=8192, G=4096, B=32) turns medians into capacity.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the workload card for P=4096, G=1024, B=16: sequences finishing per step 1/64, tokens evicted per step 80, and the cold trials (first compile, first load, first autotune) you discard before the warm median.
traps: Sweeping batch at fixed length and calling it a workload. Real prompts spread 256 to 8k with decode medians differing by 8x; fix both axes.
Warming up with the timed shapes. Autotuning on the benchmark shapes leaks tuning into the measurement; the project schema records autotuning separately from warm trials.
Keeping the first trial. First compile and allocation can exceed steady state by orders of magnitude; converge warmup first, then record.

selfTest.q: Which workload spreads does this unit cite, and why medians plus spread?
selfTest.a: LMSys-Chat-1M 417 median with 1418 p90 prefill tokens, 2k to 32k sliders, hourly runs over 24 hours. Points hide the padding, blocking and queueing that spreads cause.

selfTest.q: What belongs in cold cost but never in a warm median?
selfTest.a: Tracing and staged compilation, weight loading, allocator growth and autotuning. Warm trials start after these converge.

selfTest.q: At P=8192, G=4096, B=32, how many tokens leave the cache per step, and why?
selfTest.a: 96: B/G sequences finish per step, each evicting P+G tokens, so 32 x 12288/4096.

selfTest.q: Why did Etalon run public APIs hourly for 24 hours instead of once?
selfTest.a: Traffic and load vary through the day; one run confuses time-of-day effects with system differences.

study.title: Amdahl's law statement and derivation
study.locator: Definition and Derivation (overall speedup from optimized share and its speedup, with the worked share examples)

focus: Small batch time is weight bytes over bandwidth plus 4 latency messages per layer; large batch adds 2P operations over peak plus model-width vectors over comms bandwidth; the max assumes parallel compute and comms.
Shares come from profiles, not assumptions: attention is 8 to 31% of decode in the ESTI slice, intermediates about 10% in the FasterTransformer reconciliation.
Amdahl bounds latency at fixed workload; growing batch or chips to hide a share is a throughput argument, not a bound violation.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, bound attention work at 31% share (at most 1.45x end to end) and intermediates at 10% (at most 1.11x), then state which you would optimize for latency and why.
traps: Multiplying kernel speedup by 100% of time. A 20x attention win at 31% share is 1.4x overall; the unaccelerated 69% dominates.
Assuming overlap. The article takes the max of comms and compute; without measured overlap the honest bound is the sum.
Beating the bound by adding hardware. More chips remap the workload and change the shares; the bound holds the workload fixed.

selfTest.q: Attention is 31% of decode time and you make it infinitely fast. What is the end-to-end gain?
selfTest.a: At most \(1/(1-0.31) = 1.45\)x; the remaining 69% is untouched.

selfTest.q: Intermediates are 10% (2.2 of 22 ms). What is the most a perfect fusion earns?
selfTest.a: \(1/0.9 = 1.11\)x. Measure before fusing; a 10% share caps every fusion there.

selfTest.q: When is max(compute, comms) the wrong bound?
selfTest.a: When the stack does not overlap them. Then time is closer to the sum; state which you assumed and check a timeline.

selfTest.q: Why can't more chips push decode latency toward zero?
selfTest.a: Per-layer comms latency does not shrink with batch, so beyond some chip count it dominates; Amdahl on the serial share says the same from the other side.

units.title: Strong baselines and the correctness contract
outcomes: Choose a strong baseline (library, compiler or engine) at a matched workload and state why a weaker one would flatter the result.
Reconcile prediction with measurement by naming each residual (bandwidth efficiency, intermediates, comms, launches) with its size.
Write the correctness contract for an optimization: independent reference, tolerance policy, fallback path and consumed outputs.
units.why: A speedup against a weak baseline, or with unchecked outputs, is marketing. Strong baselines plus a correctness contract are what make a later kernel claim believable.

next.note: File the baseline and contract with the claim.

study.title: Model versus FasterTransformer reconciliation
study.locator: comparing against real benchmarks (the 1-GPU 76% and 2-GPU 62% accounting; the prefill shortfall with 72% and 54% skinny-GEMM efficiency)
study.depth: The two benchmark-run totals (180.86 ms and 283.60 ms) are reported without mapping them to the 1- and 2-GPU cases; reconcile the per-token numbers, not those totals.

study.title: Expected-versus-observed profile checks
study.locator: Looking at a real(ish) example profile (95.6 ms expected against 96 ms observed; the 128 MB ReduceScatter check)

study.title: Reference and fallback contracts
study.locator: Architecture constraints (independent references, output consumed before any speed claim, fallback for every custom path); Correctness requirements

focus: Predict first in bytes and operations (8.4 ms on 2 GPUs, 16.8 on 1), then account the gap: 90% versus 87% bandwidth, 2.2 versus 2.0 ms intermediates, 1.7 ms unparallelized comms.
Prefill shortfalls diagnose differently from decode: 72% and 54% of peak on skinny GEMMs is an efficiency finding, not a bandwidth one.
The reference never shares the target's logic, outputs are consumed before any speed claim, and every custom path keeps a fallback.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, reconcile the 1-GPU case: 16.8/0.9 = 18.6 ms plus 2.2 ms intermediates gives 20.8 ms against 22.0 measured, leaving 1.4 ms of named sub-millisecond residuals; then the 2-GPU case at 87% bandwidth.
traps: Benchmarking the totals. The reported 180.86 and 283.60 ms runs are unmapped to GPU count; reconcile per-token steps, not those totals.
Fitting constants after the fact. Each residual needs an independent line (profiled bandwidth, counted passes, timed comms); unexplained remainder stays unexplained.
Skipping output consumption. An unmaterialized or unchecked output can delete the very work you claim to time; the harness constraint exists for this.

selfTest.q: What do the 76% and 62% figures mean, and what closes each gap?
selfTest.a: Prediction over measurement per token. 1 GPU: 90% bandwidth plus 2.2 ms intermediates closes to 20.8 of 22.0. 2 GPUs: 87% bandwidth, 2.0 ms intermediates and 1.7 ms comms close to 13.4 of 13.5.

selfTest.q: Why is the prefill shortfall not a bandwidth finding?
selfTest.a: Prefill there is compute-bound, yet GEMMs reach only 72% and 54% of peak; skinny shapes underuse the matmul units, matching the cited paper's Figure 14 pattern.

selfTest.q: Why must the reference avoid sharing the target's logic?
selfTest.a: A shared bug passes both sides. Independence is what lets agreement mean correctness instead of coincidence.

selfTest.q: When is an exact match required, and when is a tolerance the contract?
selfTest.a: Exact where the math is exact (integer counts, layouts); dtype, order and conditioning set the tolerance everywhere else.

units.title: Manifests, claim schemas, predictions declared first and artifact lineage
outcomes: Write a hardware and software manifest that lets a stranger rerun one timing (device, driver, toolkit, clocks and power, config, code revision).
Declare workload, baseline, timing boundaries, prediction and falsifying signal before profiling, in a fixed claim schema.
Store raw trials, traces and generated reports with lineage from code revision to number, separating cold, warm and end-to-end invocation.
units.why: Numbers without manifests and lineage cannot be checked, so they cannot gate later work. The section checkpoint demands a versioned claim with artifacts; this unit builds that file.

next.note: Carry the manifest discipline to the training bridge.
Later serving work reuses these manifests and claim files.

study.title: Harness schema, manifest and lineage
study.locator: Core requirements (harness fields, raw samples); Architecture constraints (named timing boundaries with cold and warm separated); Measurement requirements (labeled hardware with bytes, operations and uncertainty); Milestones A and B

study.title: Declare the SLO before the sweep
study.locator: Section 4.2 (black-box and capacity recipes); Section 5.2 (the strict 25 ms SLO fixed before the QPS sweep to 0.6 capacity)

focus: Name every timing boundary (which event starts and stops each interval); asynchronous launch makes an unnamed boundary meaningless.
Predictions precede profiles: the SLO is fixed before the load sweep, and a miss moves the claim, not the target.
Raw samples are kept with environment capture; medians and uncertainty are computed from them, never quoted from a single best run.
units.reproduce: From memory, write the manifest and claim record for your unit-4 sweep: hardware, driver, toolkit, clocks and power note, workload, baseline, timing boundaries, prediction with falsifying signal, and raw-file lineage.
traps: Filing the manifest after tuning. Changed configs invalidate recorded trials; resume only under identical configuration.
Storing summaries instead of trials. A median without raw samples cannot be re-cut when the SLO changes.
Declaring the prediction after seeing the profile. A bound fitted to its own measurement predicts nothing; residuals explain, constants do not.

selfTest.q: What must a manifest contain for one GPU timing?
selfTest.a: Device model and memory, driver, toolkit and compiler versions, clocks and power capture, workload and config, timing boundaries, and the code revision behind the binary.

selfTest.q: What fields does a performance claim fix before profiling?
selfTest.a: Workload, hardware, baseline, timing boundaries, correctness method, prediction with a falsifying signal, and the artifact lineage.

selfTest.q: Why keep raw trials instead of just medians?
selfTest.a: SLOs change, and re-cutting percentiles plus uncertainty needs the samples; a single best run is not evidence at all.

selfTest.q: The sweep misses the declared SLO. What changes: the target or the claim?
selfTest.a: The claim. Moving the target after the fact turns the evaluation into a description of whatever happened.

study.title: Training problems: parameters, Adam and activation bytes, step time
study.locator: Some Problems to Work, Questions 1 to 3 with answers (13B parameters; 130 GB optimizer-state line; 42 TB checkpoint activations at 16M tokens; the 300 ms step with its comms-bound verdict)

study.title: Data-parallel and FSDP comms-bound rules
study.locator: Data Parallelism (10 bytes per parameter with Adam) and Fully-Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP) (the per-device batch over C/Wici rule with the LLaMA-3 70B 6.3e24 example)

focus: Forward is about 2ND, backward about 4ND (weight gradients plus input grads); the 6ND total shows directly in the step recomputation.
Adam in fp32 with bf16 weights costs 10 bytes per parameter (2+4+4); the 13B line is 130 GB before any activation.
Checkpoint activations scale with batch times layers (42 TB at 16M tokens); batch, not depth alone, forces the sharding choice.
FSDP and data-parallel stay compute-bound while per-device batch exceeds the interconnect ratio (2550 per axis on v5p); below it, comms sets the step.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the Question 3 step: 6 x 3e6 x 13e9 = 2.34e20 operations at 40% of 4096 x 4.6e14 gives about 310 ms (the chapter rounds to 300), and state why pure FSDP is comms-bound there.
traps: Using 2ND for a training step. Inference's forward-only count misses the backward's two matmuls per layer; the step is 6ND.
Forgetting optimizer state in the fit. The two fp32 moments cost 8 bytes against 2 for weights; parameters are a third of the 130 GB line, not all of it.
Quoting the chapter's 300 ms as exact. It rounds 310 ms at assumed 40% utilization; your utilization and hardware change the step, not the operation count.

selfTest.q: Why 6ND per training step and not 2ND?
selfTest.a: Forward costs about 2ND; backward costs about 4ND (one gradient per weight matrix plus one per input), totaling 6ND per token.

selfTest.q: How much memory do 13B bf16 parameters with fp32 Adam take, and why?
selfTest.a: (2+4+4) x 13e9 = 130 GB: 2 bytes of weight plus 4 bytes per moment accumulator.

selfTest.q: What forces sharding at 16M tokens with 3 checkpoints per layer?
selfTest.a: About 42 TB of checkpoint activations (2 x 40 x 16e6 x 5120 x 6.4 bytes); no single device holds that beside the optimizer state.

selfTest.q: Why is Question 3 comms-bound under pure FSDP?
selfTest.a: 3M tokens sit below the 3.48M minimum for 4096 chips (850 x 4096), so communication exceeds compute at that batch.
